picked.t: In Da Nang's Tam Tien, sunrise brings fish market to life
picked.body: Twenty years ago, Tam Tien Fish Market in Da Nang City was just a landing spot for fishing boats. Today, after the number of boats grew, traders began gathering there, turning it into a market. Visitors who arrive in the early morning can now see hundreds of fishing boats pull ashore at once. Khanh Phan, who lives in Ho Chi Minh City, has returned to Tam Tien Fish Market many times to capture its colors. To photograph the boats against the sun, she waits for the sun to rise red over the sea and uses a telephoto lens. Located on the coast of Ha Loc Village in Tam Xuan Commune, this summer-only market offers fresh seafood and a glimpse into local life. Photographers also frequent the market to document the lives of fishermen. "I keep coming back here year after year," Khanh says. Her last visit was in early July. Khanh usually photographs the market in two shifts: from 4:30 a.m. to 6 a.m., when returning boats make it busiest, and from 6 a.m. to 7 a.m., when trading and the morning light make for the best photos. For wide market shots, Khanh suggests arriving at around 5:15 a.m. when the sun rises. Using a wide-angle lens lets you capture the market in the foreground, boats on the water in the middle, and the sky overhead. Using a drone to capture waves crashing onto the shore is another method she enjoys. As the boats approach the shore, fishermen transfer their catch into basket boats to take ashore. Traders waiting on the beach rush to meet each basket and pick out what they want. Catches such as swordfish, grouper, and squid are then laid out for selling along the beach, drawing both locals and tourists. picked.t: Ha Giang man goes from motorbike driver to tourism entrepreneur
picked.body: In early 2023, Thuat, then 32, a native of Ha Giang (now part of Tuyen Quang Province), quit his job at a company in the Bac Ninh Industrial Park, where he was earning more than VND20 million (US$800) a month. Living far from home, facing work pressure, and feeling that the job was not a good fit, he decided to return home and look for work that would allow him to stay close to his family while offering long-term growth opportunities based on his hometown’s tourism potential. Three days after quitting, he went to Hanoi to buy a camera, spent a week studying tourist attractions and visitors’ needs, and picking the brains of some people experienced in tourism. He then began by taking tourists by motorbike to destinations such as Tham Ma Slope, Ma Pi Leng Pass, and Lo Lo Chai and shooting photos of them for free. All he asked was for them to post the photos and recommend his services to others. For the first few months, he only had three or four customers a week, and none at all sometimes. On days when he had customers, he earned VND300,000-500,000. "The hardest part was that customers did not know who I was or whether they could trust me since most of them came from southern provinces," he says. Local tourism is seasonal, with visitor numbers rising during flower and rice-harvest seasons but falling sharply during periods of heavy rain and storms. To better understand the needs of visitors, he spent time studying travel routes, checking service quality so he could offer tourists informed advice, and listening to their feedback. Finding customers through social media was also difficult because many groups required users to pay for advertising posts. Noticing that room-booking scams and misleading advertisements were becoming increasingly common as visitor numbers increased but tourists lacked a reliable source of comprehensive information, he launched the "Ha Giang Review Tat Tan Tat" (Review everything about Ha Giang) community in October 2023. The group allows members to share information about destinations and services, and accommodation providers and restaurants to promote themselves for free. To prevent misinformation, Thuat often visits businesses in person to verify information before approving posts. The community got one million members within seven months, surpassed two million in two years, and now has around 2.3 million members, a figure many KOLs long for. According to Ly Thai Chu, deputy chief of the Office of the People's Council and People's Committee of Ha Giang 2 Ward, Thuat has good understanding of tourism, is enthusiastic, and has come up with many initiatives to support local tourism. Thuat's community has grown rapidly thanks to its free, up-to-date information and its role in connecting tourists with service providers. However, its large scale also creates a need for tighter control over the accuracy of advertisements as the admin team still occasionally allows inaccurate information to slip through. Thuat said the group receives hundreds of posts and thousands of comments every day. The biggest challenge is balancing members' right to report problems with the responsibility to protect the reputations of the service providers involved. When inaccurate information is discovered, he tries to verify it quickly, issue an apology and a correction or remove the post. Ha Van Minh, a tourist from Hanoi, said the group had occasionally approved inaccurate content, such as incorrect information about when photos were taken, but "the admins are quick to correct mistakes, and so this is a tourism community I trust for information." Thuat now has seven staff members who help manage the group in shifts. After each incident, the team reviews its procedures and requires people submitting posts to provide clearer evidence. Three years after returning home, Thuat had progressed from being a motorbike taxi driver taking tourists around to managing service procurement and sales at a local travel company. At the end of 2025, he set up a company specializing in tours and transportation services for both international and domestic visitors in Tuyen Quang. The community has also raised his profile, helping increase service bookings by 50-60%. He now gets an average of 60-70 customers a day, with bookings rising by five to six times during the Lunar New Year and other holidays. Yet, whenever he has free time, he still takes his camera to tourist attractions across Tuyen Quang to photograph visitors for free just as he did three years ago. Thuat's current income is 1.5 to two times what he earned while working in Bac Ninh. What means the most to him, however, are the messages of thanks from tourists he has advised and protected from scammers. Chu Thuy Linh of Hanoi once nearly lost almost VND10 million after booking a non-existent hotel. picked.t: Nam A Bank secures $60M from FMO for green finance, small businesses
picked.body: The signing ceremony on Sept. 25 was attended by Hanna Pors, Deputy Consul General of the Netherlands in Ho Chi Minh City, along with senior representatives of Nam A Bank and FMO. The agreement further reinforces Nam A Bank's reputation, international- standard governance capabilities and commitment to sustainable development. Under the agreement, Nam A Bank will prioritize green projects while expanding lending to micro enterprises and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). The five-year loan will support agriculture, agricultural value chains and rural development, as well as farmers and businesses owned or led by women and young people. The financing is also intended to improve access to longer-term funding for businesses facing financing constraints and support companies seeking to reduce emissions, respond to climate change and adopt more sustainable production models. Vo Hoang Hai, Deputy CEO of Nam A Bank, said the financing would allow the bank to expand green lending and the social impact of its credit activities. "The financing from FMO will be directed toward customer groups that still have considerable unmet financing needs, allowing the bank to expand its social impact alongside its green growth objectives," Hai said. "It is also the result of years of building credibility and reflects Nam A Bank's strategy of diversifying its international funding sources." Frouke Hoekstra, Director of Financial Institutions at FMO, said the partnership supports two of the development bank's priorities: the green transition and access to finance for underserved businesses. "By providing long-term financing for green projects, micro enterprises and SMEs, including women- and youth-owned businesses, we aim to support a more sustainable and inclusive private sector in Vietnam," she said. Hanna Pors, Deputy Consul General of the Netherlands in Ho Chi Minh City, said Vietnam-Netherlands cooperation is increasingly moving from experience sharing toward developing long-term solutions for sustainable development, with green finance playing a growing role. She said the agreement could help translate international capital, expertise and networks into development opportunities in Vietnam, while supporting Nam A Bank's efforts to strengthen ties with international financial institutions. The agreement follows an ESG forum held in Hanoi on Sept. 22 by the Embassy of the Netherlands in Vietnam and FMO. The "ESG Insights for Banking Leaders" event brought together senior executives from FMO's partner banks to discuss integrating environmental, social and governance (ESG) risk management into board-level decisions. The FMO financing follows another international credit agreement signed by Nam A Bank earlier this month. On Sept. 9, the bank secured a $30 million credit facility from French development finance institution Proparco for green finance, bringing its international financing signed in September to $90 million. Nam A Bank has been expanding its green credit portfolio and integrating an Environmental and Social Management System (ESMS) into its lending operations. The bank said international financing has supported longer-term funding for renewable energy, high-tech agriculture and SMEs. FMO is the Dutch entrepreneurial development bank, investing in private-sector projects in developing and emerging markets. It focuses on areas including agribusiness, food and forestry, energy and financial institutions. FMO has more than 55 years of experience and a committed portfolio of approximately €16 billion across more than 85 countries.
